A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. The core algorithm, theoretical results, original experiments, and appendix proofs can be matched reliably; text and rendered figures and tables are readable.

before.justification: Section IV reports original reward-machine recovery experiments, solution counts, and SAT timings for grid-world and block-stacking tasks.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report retained experiments plus original finite-demonstration simulations, robotic-arm evaluations, and reward-machine inference from existing mouse-trajectory data.

M1.justification: V2 adds a finite-demonstration learning procedure: empirical prefix-tree policy estimation, confidence-based selection of negative examples, and weighted MAX-SAT with soft negative-example constraints. V1 assumes an exact finite-depth policy and uses hard SAT; that original procedure is retained.

E1.justification: V2 retains the four grid-world and BlockWorld tasks and adds continuous-state robotic-arm target sequencing and real water-restricted mouse navigation. These introduce substantially different environments and a biological population. Sampled demonstrations of retained BlockWorld tasks do not themselves constitute new task coverage.

E2.justification: Section 5.3 adds comparisons against hard SAT and a control using ground-truth filtering of false negative-example labels. Appendix B.3 adds a uniformly random policy reference for mouse policy fit. These are limited internal and reference comparisons absent from v1.

E3.justification: The stated common discount factor changes from 0.9 to 0.99; unchanged inherited table values do not establish rerunning. New experiments introduce finite-trajectory sampling, demonstration-count and threshold settings, PPO training and state/action discretization, and false-positive and policy-fit metrics.

E4.justification: V2 adds demonstration-size sensitivity for both BlockWorld tasks (Tables 4-5), threshold and false-positive analyses with SAT/MAX-SAT controls for Reacher (Table 3), and mouse model-size comparisons (Appendix B.3). It also examines specific unresolved transition ambiguities. The original non-stuttering ablation remains.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 newly introduces confidence bounds and an alpha threshold for deciding whether sampled action distributions differ. This quantifies uncertainty within learning. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or performance error bars.

E6.justification: Original Table I entries are retained in Tables 1-2. New results include two stack solutions versus four stack-avoid solutions with one million demonstrations, four MAX-SAT assignments despite hard-SAT infeasibility on Reacher, and mouse policy-fit norms of 2.66 versus 2.97 for a uniform policy. These are newly reported outcomes, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: The finite-depth recovery theorem, propositions, and appendix proofs are retained. Section 4 adds an empirical-policy definition and a concentration-bound/union-bound argument for negative-example confidence. This is a limited mathematical extension; it does not supply an end-to-end finite-sample recovery theorem.

C1.justification: V1 presents recovery from an exact finite-depth prefix-tree policy and leaves finite demonstrations to future work. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim learning directly from demonstrations and robustness to policy-estimation errors, substantially broadening the contribution while retaining the exact-policy guarantee.

C2.justification: V2 clarifies that topology learning requires neither policy optimality nor known transition probabilities, unlike numerical reward recovery. It adds substantive discussion of persistent sampling ambiguities, hydration/exploration interpretations for mice, and sparse-data/model mismatch that prevents exact reward-based policy reconstruction (Appendix B).

D1.justification: Appendix B adds simulation pseudocode, PPO training for 20 million steps with 50 CPU environments, discretization and sampling instructions, and mouse-policy clipping at 0.05. Conversely, v1's explicit code URL is replaced by a promise of release upon acceptance, reducing direct code-access information.

R1.justification: V2 retains the earlier literature and central novelty positioning while adding references supporting confidence bounds, MAX-SAT, robotic simulation, and animal-behavior analysis, including Weissman, Manquinho, Rosenberg, and Ashwood. The related-work argument is supplemented rather than substantially redefined.

P1.justification: The title drops 'Optimal', terminology and explanatory passages are refined, experiments gain domain-specific subsections, and proofs are grouped under Appendix A. Much of the original introduction, preliminaries, algorithm explanation, and proof narrative remains closely matched.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column format with a single-column layout, consolidates original illustrations into multipart figures, and splits Table I by domain. It adds substantial displays for Reacher, mouse navigation, and finite-data ambiguities, while retaining the original proof illustration under new numbering.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves finite-demonstration learning to future work. V2 implements and evaluates that extension, adds continuous and real-data applications, and diagnoses sampling ambiguities, substantially strengthening practical support for the framework. The exact-policy theorem remains limited to its original setting, and the explicit code link becomes a future-release promise, but these limitations do not outweigh the methodological and evidential gains.
